title: Independence or Autonomy: Pale Crystallizes Its Path
content:
Between the Pale assembly's rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan in May 1993 and the looming Contact Group framework of 1994, the Bosnian Serb leadership had to settle a foundational question of posture: was the Republika Srpska a state-in-waiting pursuing full independence and eventual union with Serbia, or a self-governing entity that would, under sufficient pressure, accept a negotiated place inside a reconstituted Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The question was never abstract. Radovan Karadžić, Momčilo Krajišnik, and Ratko Mladić conferred at Pale across the autumn of 1993 and into 1994 under steadily diverging pressures. Slobodan Milošević, managing Belgrade's own exposure to the UNSCR 820 sanctions tightened in April 1993, signalled with growing insistence that the RS should bank its territorial gains and accept a settlement. The Pale leadership, holding roughly 70 percent of Bosnian territory and committed since the May 1992 Bosanski Šamac assembly session to its Six Strategic Goals, resisted any framework that subordinated the RS to a Sarajevo-centred state.

The ICTY record at Krajišnik and Karadžić documents this as a recurring choice rather than a single decision: each diplomatic envelope — Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg, the Contact Group map — forced Pale to re-state where on the spectrum from independence to reintegration it stood. Historically the leadership held to the rejectionist, independence-seeking line until the combined shock of Operation Storm, NATO's Operation Deliberate Force, and Milošević's assumption of the negotiating mandate at Dayton overrode it.

The posture chosen here is the hinge on which much of the RS war turns: it conditions the Belgrade relationship, the willingness to absorb military pressure rather than negotiate, and the terms on which the war could end.
